com: New, by their form and qualities, but not by their substance. — The first heaven and first earth was passed away: being changed, not as to their substance, but in their qualities. (Challoner)

Coming down from God out of heaven. By the city we must understand its citizens, the Angels and saints. (Witham) — Justice, innocence, the good works of the saints, are the ornaments of the inhabitants of this new Jerusalem, the Church triumphant. If the world of the old Adam has appeared so beautiful, so magnificent, good God, what will be the riches of that which is made for Jesus Christ, the second Adam, and for his members! O Jesus! Father of the world to come, render us worthy of this new and everlasting world, and give us a disgust, a mortal hatred, for that which perishes, and which is the cause of our perdition.
Behold the tabernacle of God with men, inasmuch as God’s elect shall there dwell with him for ever and ever. (Witham)

It is done. The state of Christ’s Church on earth, and in this world, is now finished; and the time is come to reward the good, and to punish the wicked in the lake burning with fire and brimstone, in hell, with the devils for all eternity. (Witham) — This living water is God himself, of which the saints shall be inebriated at the source; i.e. in God himself. Enviable moment, when all the designs of God upon Jesus Christ and upon his Church will be accomplished: but how little thought of now! And how can we hope to be inebriated at this source of God above, if we do not aspire after it whilst we are in this dreary desert here below? He who begins and finishes gratuitously here below the work of our faith, crowns it still more liberally in heaven.
I will shew thee the bride, the wife of the Lamb: all the Church triumphant in heaven. (Witham)
The city is situate four-square;[1] and by what follows, so as to be a perfect square, though every thing that is quadrangular is not always a square, or perfect square. (Witham)
The measure of a man, which is of an Angel.[2] This seems, without doubt, the sense of it. (Witham)

No temple in it. No need of a temple for divine worship, where God is in such a perfect manner present to all the blessed, where nothing can distract or divert their souls from endless adorations, praises, &c. (Witham)
Needeth not sun nor moon, where there is no vicissitude or succession of day and night, the divine brightness always shining to them. (Witham)

The kings of the earth shall bring their glory; the elect, of all states and conditions, shall now be exalted like kings, or rather infinitely above the glory that we can imagine of any kings in this world. (Witham)
There shall not enter it any thing defiled. This is what we ought always to remember and have in our minds. (Witham)
The first heaven and the first earth was gone ... being changed, not as to their substance, but in their qualities.
The measure of a man, i.e., According to the measure of men, and used by the angel.... This seems to be the true meaning of these words.
fa: Irenaeus Against Heresies Book 5
Against Heresies Book V

… Isaiah also declares the very same: "For there shall be a new heaven and a new earth; and there shall be no remembrance of the former, neither shall the heart think about them, but they shall find in it joy and exultation. Now this is what has been said by the apostle: "For the fashion of this world passeth away. To the same purpose did the Lord also declare, "Heaven and earth shall pass away. When these things, therefore, pass away above the earth, John, the Lord's disciple, says that the new Jerusalem above shall [then] descend, as a bride adorned for her husband; and that this is the tabernacle of God, in which God will dwell with men.
Dubious and Spurious Pieces
Dubious Hippolytus Fragments

… For the river of fire shall come forth in fury like an angry sea, and shall burn up mountains and hills, and shall make the sea vanish, and shall dissolve the atmosphere with its heat like wax. The stars of heaven shall fall, the sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood. The heaven shall be rolled together like a scroll: the whole earth shall be burnt up by reason of the deeds done in it, which men did corruptly, in fornications, in adulteries, and in lies and uncleanness, and in idolatries, and in murders, and in battles. For there shall be the new heaven and the new earth.
Against Hermogenes

"Heaven and earth shall pass away," says He. "The first heaven and the first earth passed away," "and there was found no place for them," because, of course, that which comes to an end loses locality.
Against Hermogenes

Even" the sea shall be no more." Now if any person should go so far as to suppose that all these passages ought to be spiritually interpreted, he will yet be unable to deprive them of the true accomplishment of those issues which must come to pass just as they have been written For all figures of speech necessarily arise out of real things, not out of chimerical ones; t because nothing is capable of imparting anything of its own for a similitude, except it actually be that very thing which it imparts in the similitude.
Commentary on Revelation

… Alternatively, the sea will no longer exist because it will lose its present form, as will heaven and earth, and be restored in a more beautiful form. But I think this should be understood spiritually as well: everything said about the renewal of heaven and earth should be understood both historically, as we said above, and spiritually. Therefore, by heaven we may understand the souls of the saints, and by earth, their bodies. Heaven will be made new when the souls of the saints, through the reception of their bodies, are restored to human nature and form. Earth will be made new when the bodies of the saints, which were once mortal and corruptible, are made immortal and incorruptible. …
Irenaeus Against Heresies Book 5
Against Heresies Book V

… He does not say this with any thought of an erratic Aeon, or of any other power which departed from the Pleroma, or of Prunicus, but of the Jerusalem which has been delineated on [God's] hands. And in the Apocalypse John saw this new [Jerusalem] descending upon the new earth.
Irenaeus Against Heresies Book 5
Against Heresies Book V

When these things, therefore, pass away above the earth, John, the Lord's disciple, says that the new Jerusalem above shall [then] descend, as a bride adorned for her husband; and that this is the tabernacle of God, in which God will dwell with men. Of this Jerusalem the former one is an image-that Jerusalem of the former earth in which the righteous are disciplined beforehand for incorruption and prepared for salvation. And of this tabernacle Moses received the pattern in the mount; and nothing is capable of being allegorized, but all things are stedfast, and true, and substantial, having been made by God for righteous men's enjoyment. …
The Five Books Against Marcion
Book 3

But we do confess that a kingdom is promised to us upon the earth, although before heaven, only in another state of existence; inasmuch as it will be after the resurrection for a thousand years in the divinely-built city of Jerusalem, "let down from heaven," which the apostle also calls "our mother from above; " and, while declaring that our poli/teuma, or citizenship, is in heaven, he predicates of it that it is really a city in heaven.
Commentary on Revelation

And I saw the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband. The city of Jerusalem is the Church, built from all the righteous; it will come down from heaven, because when the Lord comes for judgment, the whole multitude of the saints will come with him, as the prophet Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judge with the elders of his people and its princes” (Isa. 3:14). And the wisest Solomon says in Proverbs: “Her husband is renowned at the city gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31:23). …
Commentary on Revelation

And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, God’s dwelling is with humanity, and he will dwell with them; they will be his people, and the Lord himself will be with them as their God.” We know that Jerusalem and the Lord’s dwelling are often used to signify the Church. Therefore, in this passage, the city and the dwelling are called the Church, because God dwells in it, as he says through the prophet: “I will dwell among them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Lev. 26:12).
On the Resurrection of the Flesh
ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 58

If sorrow, and mourning, and sighing and death itself assail us from the afflictions both of soul and body, how shall they be removed, except by the cessation of their causes, that is to say, the afflictions of flesh and soul? Where will you find adversities in the presence of God? Where incursions of an enemy in the bosom of Christ? Where attacks of the devil in the face of the Holy Spirit—now that the devil himself and his angels are "cast into the lake of fire"? Where now is necessity, and what [the pagans] call fortune or fate? What plague awaits the redeemed from death after their eternal pardon? What wrath is there for the reconciled after grace? …
On the Resurrection of the Flesh

The angel echoes the same to John: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; " from the same eyes indeed which had formerly wept, and which might weep again, if the loving-kindness of God did not dry up every fountain of tears. And again: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death," and therefore no more corruption, it being chased away by incorruption, even as death is by immortality.
On Modesty

Yet I must necessarily prescribe you a law, not to stretch out your hand after the old things, not to look backwards: for "the old things are passed away," according to Isaiah; and "a renewing hath been renewed," according to Jeremiah; and "forgetful of former things, we are reaching forward," according to the apostle; and "the law and the prophets (were) until John," according to the Lord.
Commentary on Revelation

… It seems to me that Solomon spoke of these two periods when he said: “A time to weep, and a time to laugh” (Eccles. 3:2). The time for the chosen to weep is now; the time to laugh will be then, when what the Lord says in the Gospel is fulfilled: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). But to sinners he says: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will weep and mourn! (Luke 6:25). Therefore God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, because after the resurrection nothing sorrowful can happen to them from which tears could arise.
Commentary on Revelation

And death shall be no more. The first man was made immortal; but by sinning he lost immortality and brought death into the world. After the resurrection, however, there will be no death, because the Devil himself, the prince of death, will be kept forever in hell [infernum] with all his followers, and the immortality that the first man lost by sinning will be restored to the righteous. The ability to sin, which brought death into the world, will also be taken away from them.
Irenaeus Against Heresies Book 5
Against Heresies Book V

… For as it is God truly who raises up man, so also does man truly rise from the dead, and not allegorically, as I have shown repeatedly. And as he rises actually, so also shall he be actually disciplined beforehand for incorruption, and shall go forwards and flourish in the times of the kingdom, in order that he may be capable of receiving the glory of the Father. Then, when all things are made new, he shall truly dwell in the city of God. For it is said, "He that sitteth on the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And the Lord says, Write all this; for these words are faithful and true. …
Commentary on Revelation
And he who sat on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” We have said something above about the renewal of creatures.
Commentary on Revelation
And he said to me, “Write, for these words are most faithful and true.” But this, too, was said above.
Treatise 12. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews
Treatise XII Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

… I have glorified Thee on the earth: I have finished the work which Thou gavest me to do. And now, do Thou glorify me with Thyself, with the glory which I had with Thee before the world was made. Also Paul to the Colossians: "Who is the image of the invisible God, and the first-born of every creature. Also in the same place: "The first-born from the dead, that He might in all things become the holder of the pre-eminence. In the Apocalypse too: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto Him that is thirsting from the fountain of the water of life freely. …
Treatise 12. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews
Treatise XII Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

… Also in the Apocalypse: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end I will give to him that is athirst, of the fountain of living water freely. He that overcometh shall possess these things, and their inheritance; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. Also in the eighty-first Psalm: "God stood in the congregation of gods, and judging gods in the midst. And again in the same place: "I have said, Ye are gods; and ye are all the children of the Highest: but ye shall die like men. …
The Stromata Book 6

The sensible types of these, then, are the sounds we pronounce. Thus the Lord Himself is called "Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end," "by whom all things were made, and without whom not even one thing was made." God's resting is not, then, as some conceive, that God ceased from doing. For, being good, if He should ever cease from doing good, then would He cease from being God, which it is sacrilege even to say. The resting is, therefore, the ordering that the order of created things should be preserved inviolate, and that each of the creatures should cease from the ancient disorder.
Pseudo-Tertullian
Appendix. Against All Heresies

After these there were not wanting a Marcus and a Colarbasus, composing a novel heresy out of the Greek alphabet. For they affirm that without those letters truth cannot be found; nay more, that in those letters the whole plenitude and perfection of truth is comprised; for this was why Christ said, "I am the Alpha and the Omega." In fact, they say that Jesus Christ descended, that is, that the dove came down on Jesus; and, since the dove is styled by the Greek name peristera (peristera), it has in itself this number DCCCI.
Commentary on Revelation
And he said to me, “I am the Alpha and the Omega.” He explains what Alpha and Omega mean by adding,
(untitled)

Let those who are hungry come, that being fed with heavenly food, they may lay aside their lasting hunger; let those who are athirst come, that they may with full mouth draw forth the water of salvation from an ever-flowing fountain.
Commentary on Revelation

The one who conquers will inherit these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son. The one who conquers the Devil, overcomes every vice, and perseveres in good works will inherit these things, that is, what was said above: namely, that he himself will drink from the fountain of eternal life, which is everlasting glory.
Scorpiace
"But the fearful," says John-and then come the others-" will have their part in the lake of fire and brimstone." Thus fear, which, as stated in his epistle, love drives out, has punishment.
On Modesty

In short, this Apocalypse, in its later passages, has assigned "the infamous and fornicators," as well as "the cowardly, and unbelieving, and murderers, and sorcerers, and idolaters," who have been guilty of any such crime while professing the faith, to "the lake of fire," without any conditional condemnation.
On Flight in Persecution
Last of all, in the Revelation, He does not propose flight to the "fearful," but a miserable portion among the rest of the outcast, in the lake of brimstone and fire, which is the second death.
Commentary on Revelation

But as for the cowardly, the unbelieving, the accursed, murderers, the fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake of burning sulfur, which is the second death. Since fear is very necessary for people, why did he place fear first among the eight very worst vices? There are good fears and bad fears. There is a very good fear, of which the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever” (Ps. 18:10). There is also the very necessary fear of death and the fear of eternal fire; and there is the fear of good people, when they are loved by those who fear them. …
Treatise 12. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews
Treatise XII Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

… Also in Jeremiah: "And I will take away from the cities of Judah, and from the streets of Jerusalem, the voice of the joyous, and the voice of the glad; the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride. Also in the eighteenth Psalm: "And he is as a bridegroom going forth from his chamber; he exulted as a giant to run his course. From the height of heaven is his going forth, and his circuit even to the end of it; and there is nothing which is hid from his heat. Also in the Apocalypse: "Come, I will show thee the new bride, the Lamb's wife. …
Commentary on Revelation

The seventh vision, which by the Lord’s gift we have reached, concerns completely the time that will follow the resurrection (above in chapter 15). The order of the account required that, after describing the general resurrection, he should describe the glory of the saints, which they will possess without end after the resurrection; in this vision it is portrayed under the figure of the city of Jerusalem.
Commentary on Revelation

And one of the seven angels who had the bowls came and spoke to me, saying: “Come, and I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” Earlier, in the fifth vision, (Rev. 17) John says that he was shown seven angels holding seven bowls, and later that one of them showed him the city of the devil and its condemnation in the form of a prostitute. Likewise, here he says that one of those same seven angels showed him the city of God in the figure of Jerusalem. …
The Five Books Against Marcion
Book 3

This both Ezekiel had knowledge of and the Apostle John beheld. And the word of the new prophecy which is a part of our belief, attests how it foretold that there would be for a sign a picture of this very city exhibited.
Commentary on Revelation

And he carried me to a great and lofty mountain. This mountain is Christ. The Prophet speaks of this mountain, saying: “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established above the tops of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). The mountains above whose tops the mountain of the house of the Lord is said to be established signify the Fathers of the Old Testament. Therefore the mountain of the house of the Lord is said to be established above their tops because they themselves foretold him, and when he came in the flesh, he surpassed them by a wondrous height. …
Commentary on Revelation

And he showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God. It should be noted that Ezekiel’s final vision agrees in some places with this vision of John; therefore, it pleased us to insert a few things from that vision into this work. For he says (Ezek. 40:2) that a mountain was shown to him, on which stood a city, and within it a temple. Although he mentions only the city, he speaks at length about the structure of the temple. The temple there therefore has the same meaning as the city here, for both signify the Church. …
Commentary on Revelation

It is also said that the city had the glory of God. Indeed, it had God’s glory, not its own. For the sun often shines upon water and lends its brightness to it, so that the water dazzles the eyes of those who look upon it just as the sun does. Therefore, just as water has the sun’s brightness, not from itself but from the sun, so the saints have God’s glory, not from themselves but from God, by whom they are enlightened.
Commentary on Revelation

Its radiance was like a precious stone, like jasper, like crystal. Behold, he set three stones, to whose radiance he compared the light of the Church: one without a name, but naming the other two. Therefore we can understand the Father as the precious stone, the Son as jasper, and the Holy Spirit as crystal. The first is unnamed because the Father is from himself; the second and third are named because the Son is from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. We can also understand hope as the precious stone, faith as jasper, and love as crystal. But someone might say that faith and hope will not be needed in that life. …
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

In that he says there are three gates placed on each of the four sides, of single pearls, I think that these are the four virtues, to wit, prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance, which are associated with one another. And, being involved together, they make the number twelve. But the twelve gates we believe to be the number of the apostles, who, shining in the four virtues as precious stones, manifesting the light of their doctrine among the saints, cause it to enter the celestial city, that by intercourse with them the choir of angels may be gladdened.
Commentary on Revelation

And it had a great and high wall. This is the wall of which the prophet says: “Our strong city is Zion; the Savior shall be set within it as a wall and fortification” (Isa. 26:1). By this wall, therefore, Christ is signified together with all his members, so that its foundation represents him, while the rest of its structure represents his members.
Commentary on Revelation

Having twelve gates. In Ezekiel (Ezek. 46:1 and so on) it is written that the temple shown to him had three gates: the eastern, the southern, and the northern. God commands that the eastern gate always remain shut, with only the Prince entering and leaving through it. The eastern gate represents the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, who remained shut before the Prince, that is, Christ, entered, and remained shut forever after he left. The southern gate represents the Old Testament, while the northern gate represents the New. Those said to come from the south represent the Jews; those from the north represent the Gentiles. …
Commentary on Revelation

And I saw twelve angels at the gates. The twelve angels represent the other preachers, namely, the followers of the apostles, who are said to have been at the gates because, holding fast to the unwavering faith of the apostles and following their teaching, they strove to draw as many people as they could to faith in Christ.
Commentary on Revelation

And the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel were written there. By the names of the twelve tribes we may understand the fathers of the Old Testament, who did not stray from faith in the Holy Trinity; we may also understand the Old Testament itself by those same names. The names of the twelve tribes were written on the gates because the teaching of the apostles and the other preachers is full of examples from the Old Testament.
Commentary on Revelation

Three gates on the east, three gates on the north, three gates on the south, and three gates on the west. He set out the four quarters of the world to show that nearly all the nations contained within those four quarters had come together in the Church. He said that he saw three gates facing each quarter, twelve in all, to show that no one can enter the Church except through confession of the Holy Trinity. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the city wall had twelve foundations, and written on them were the twelve names of the apostles and of the Lamb. He explained what the twelve foundations signified when he added that the names of the twelve apostles and of the Lamb were written on them. I was rebuked by someone for saying that Peter was the foundation of the Church, in the passage where the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). If Peter is the foundation of the Church, as are the other apostles, as the present passage plainly shows, then the Church was built upon him, just as it was upon the others. …
Commentary on Revelation

… 11:30). Therefore the iron rod will be changed into a light, sweet, and golden reed, because the saints will receive sweetness and everlasting glory in return for the hardships they endured for Christ. He will measure the city, its gates, and its wall when he repays each person according to the quality of their deeds. But we must ask: since the city is said to have been measured, why are its gates and wall added, when all these are included in the name “city”? Yet, as what came before and what follows show, the gates signify the apostles, the city signifies apostolic men, and the walls signify the remaining multitude of the faithful. What follows makes this clearer. Next:
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

The city which he says is squared, he says also is resplendent with gold and precious stones, and has a sacred street, and a river through the midst of it, and the tree of life on either side, bearing twelve manner of fruits throughout the twelve months; and that the light of the sun is not there, because the Lamb is the light of it; and that its gates were of single pearls; and that there were three gates on each of the four sides, and that they could not be shut. I say, in respect of the square city, he shows forth the united multitude of the saints, in whom the faith could by no means waver. …
Commentary on Revelation

… We have said all this about the square stone to show that the city’s square shape signifies the perfection of the Church. And because this city has equal sides, its length is said to be as great as its width. For its length signifies eternal glory, while its width signifies love. The length of this city, then, is as great as its width, because the greater each believer’s love in this life, the greater the glory they will possess in heavenly blessedness; and the lesser their love, the lesser their glory.
Commentary on Revelation

And he measured the city at twelve thousand stadia: its length, width, and height are equal. The twelve stadia have the same meaning as the twelve gates, for they signify the apostles. Above, however, it is said that the city has equal length and width; here it is said that its length, width, and height are equal. Therefore, by these three things mentioned here, we may understand faith, hope, and love: by length, faith; by width, love; and by height, hope. But how can they be equal, when the Apostle says, “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Cor. 13:13)? …
Commentary on Revelation

And he measured its wall: one hundred and forty-four cubits, by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement. If we consider what was said earlier, this cannot stand literally. For earlier he says that he measured the city at twelve stadia, whereas here he says that the city’s walls were measured at one hundred and forty-four cubits. The distance of twelve stadia is much greater than that of one hundred and forty-four cubits. Therefore, by the greater distance we can understand those of greater merit. Earlier we said that the twelve apostles were represented by the twelve stadia. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the structure of its wall was jasper; the city itself was like pure gold, like clear glass. Here, too, he made some distinction between the walls and the city. He said that the walls were built of jasper, while the city itself was like pure gold and clear glass. For the green manner of jasper signifies faith; therefore, jasper rightly represents all simple and imperfect men, who are saved through faith, as the prophet says: “The righteous shall live by his faith” (Hab. 2:4). …
Commentary on Revelation

The foundations of the city wall are adorned with every precious stone. We said above that the twelve foundations represent the twelve apostles; all the righteous, however, are represented by the precious stones. Therefore, the twelve foundations will be adorned with twelve stones, because in that blessedness the apostles and the other preachers will have as their adornment those who believed through them, since they will receive their reward on behalf of all of them.
Commentary on Revelation

The first foundation is jasper. Jasper is green and a deep color; it signifies worldly believers who abstain from vices, although their greenness, that is, their faith, is somewhat clouded by worldly pursuits. Nevertheless, they do not cease to redeem their sins through almsgiving and other works of mercy. Nor is it without reason that such people are placed first: the apostles, as has often already been emphasized, were afraid to lay harsher commandments of the Lord upon those among the Gentiles who had only recently believed, lest they be frightened by the severity of the commandments and not dare to come forward to embrace the faith of Christ. …
Commentary on Revelation

The second sapphire. Sapphire is blue in color, like hyacinth, but it has drops sprinkled throughout it of the same color, though darker. It seems to me that certain worldly men are also represented by this stone: they long for heavenly things, yet are still occupied with worldly affairs, from which occupation they seem to acquire certain stains. Because they put heavenly things above all concerns, they are said to have the color of heaven. They are placed second in number because they strive to love God above all things and their neighbors as themselves.
Commentary on Revelation

The third is the chalcedony. Chalcedony is red in color, yet dark unless it is made thin by cutting; the hollow itself, however, gives it a most beautiful and pleasing color. This stone also signifies certain worldly men whose great holiness before the time of persecution had gone unnoticed. But when they were worn down by their persecutors through various tribulations, the full splendor of the holiness hidden within them became clear to all. They are fittingly placed in the third place, because, unwavering in their confession of the Holy Trinity, they deserved to achieve the honor of martyrdom.
Commentary on Revelation

The fourth, an emerald. The emerald is of exceptional beauty and greenness, so much so that it tinges with its own green everything around it. It represents holy preachers, green in faith and distinguished by their virtues, who spread the radiance of their faith everywhere through their preaching. They are therefore placed in the fourth place, because they spread the teaching of the Gospel, which is divided into four books, across many places.
Commentary on Revelation

Fifth, sardonyx. Sardonyx is white, tending slightly toward red: it signifies all the simple and innocent men, who are represented by the white stone because of the purity of their lives. Since, by keeping vigil, fasting, abstaining, and afflicting their bodies in various ways, they impose martyrdoms upon themselves, they seem to have a reddish manner. They are appropriately placed in the fifth place, for the five senses of the body are often represented by the number five. Blessed Gregory also says that the knowledge of external things is represented by the five bodily senses. …
Commentary on Revelation

Sixth, the sardius. The sardius is yellowish-brown in color, and because it seems to incline somewhat toward red, it is slightly darkened. The yellowish-brown manner, which approaches the color of gold, therefore signifies the tribulations the saints endured at the hands of their enemies; the red color signifies martyrdom. Therefore the sardius signifies holy and perfect men who, after experiencing every virtue, enduring various persecutions and suffering enormous torments at the hands of their enemies, were deemed worthy to achieve the honor of martyrdom. They are correctly placed under the number six, which is perfect, because they were perfect in virtue and crowned that perfection with martyrdom.
Commentary on Revelation

Seventh, the chrysolite. The chrysolite is entirely golden, and wisdom is often represented by gold. Therefore, the chrysolite represents wise men in the Church, who, because of the radiance of their wisdom, may rightly be called golden among men. They are fittingly placed in the seventh place, because, filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, they have turned many away from wickedness through their words and examples.
Commentary on Revelation

The eighth is beryl. Beryl is of exceptional brilliance, with a blue manner blended into it. It signifies people of pure lives, wholly removed from the deeds of the world. So that they might not in any way stain the radiance of their lives, they even chose to separate themselves from the company of other people. Their radiance turned blue, because they are shown to have led an angelic life among people, with their minds ever fixed on heaven. They are fittingly placed in the eighth place, for twice four makes eight. …
Commentary on Revelation

The ninth is topaz. Topaz is said to be the color of bronze and gold, spreading its radiance all around. Proven men are often represented by gold: those tested in the fire of tribulation. The tribulations themselves are various. At times, holy men are tested by the different temptations they suffer from demons; at times, by tribulations inflicted on them by evil people; at times, by afflictions they impose upon themselves; at times, they are tested by God’s scourges, and by the disciplines of the active life. It therefore seems to me that the stone topaz represents those who are first tested through the works of the active life and afterward pass on to the contemplative life. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate made from a single pearl. This cannot hold literally. If each gate was made from a single pearl, how can it be said that there were twelve pearls at each of the twelve gates? But it must be understood spiritually: there are twelve pearls, from which the individual gates are said to be made, that is, one hundred and forty-four. These signify the Church’s teachers, successors to the apostles, who followed the apostles’ faith and teaching and imitated their deeds. Because of the purity and exceptional holiness of their lives, they are represented by the whiteness of pearls.
Commentary on Revelation

And the street of the city was pure gold, like see-through glass. Earlier, we said that perfect men and holy angels were signified by pure gold and clear glass. But here, the street of the city signifies the minds of the faithful, while pure gold and see-through glass represent the purity of human and angelic minds. For just as no vain thought could ever enter the minds of angels and stain them, so after the resurrection no useless thought will ever come to the saints and defile their minds.
Commentary on Revelation

And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. The temple, in which offerings and sacrifices were made, signifies the present Church, in which not bodily but spiritual sacrifices are offered to God every day. For just as the rite of sacrifice was practiced there according to the kinds of sins, so in the Church the sacrifices of repentance, prayer, tears, and remorse of heart must correspond to the measure of one’s faults. The Prophet speaks of such sacrifices, saying: “A remorseful spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50:19); and again: “Then you will accept a sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. 50:21). …
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

And in that he says that the sun is not necessary in the city, he shows, evidently, that the Creator as the immaculate light shines in the midst of it, whose brightness no mind has been able to conceive, nor tongue to tell.
Commentary on Revelation

And the city has no need of the sun or the moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb. The New Testament is signified by the sun, the Old Testament by the moon. Without these two lights, the Church cannot walk the path of righteousness through the darkness of this age without frequent stumbling. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. By the nations are meant all the elect. But how will they walk? They will walk in mind, not in body: not by changing their place, but by contemplating omnipotence, divinity, and majesty. They will walk by the light of the Church, because, to complete this journey, they will be enlightened by that light which almighty God will give to the whole Church. By the kings of the earth are meant the apostles and the other preachers. …
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

And that the gates cannot be shut, it is evidently shown that the doctrine of the apostles can be separated from rectitude by no tempest of contradiction. Even though the floods of the nations and the vain superstitions of heretics should revolt against their true faith, they are overcome, and shall be dissolved as the foam, because Christ is the Rock by which, and on which, the Church is founded. And thus it is overcome by no traces of maddened men.
Commentary on Revelation

And its gates shall not be shut by day, for there will be no night there. Above, we said that the twelve apostles were represented by the twelve gates said to have been made of twelve pearls. But here, where the gates are mentioned without number, they have another meaning: they signify the hearts of the faithful. For the faithful, while living in this life, endure night, that is, demons and wicked people. They shut the gates at night when, against every temptation of demons, they lock the entrances to their minds and drive such temptations away. …
Commentary on Revelation

And they will bring the glory of the nations and their honor into it. Above, he says that the kings of the earth, that is, the holy preachers, brought their glory into the holy city; by that glory, as we have said, the nations who believed through them were signified. If, then, the glory of the preachers is the nations, what is the nations’ glory? Perhaps we should understand this according to Solomon, who says: “The glory of the aged is their children’s children, and the glory of children is their fathers” (Prov. 17:6). …
Commentary on Revelation

Nothing defiled shall enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life. He calls defiled those who have defiled themselves with various crimes; those who do evil, however, practice abomination. For God hates nothing except wickedness, as it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “You have mercy on all, O Lord, and hate none of the things you have made” (Wisdom 11:25). But one may ask why it is said that falsehood is practiced. What we do is no longer falsehood, because what has been done cannot remain undone so as to be falsehood. …
ftr: John Litteral, released into the public domain
